description: ABRET Challenge Bank batch 8: ICU, continuous EEG, electrocerebral inactivity and encephalopathy (ACNS 2021 terminology). Not yet medically verified.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old ICU patient had a 9-Hz posterior dominant rhythm yesterday. Today, 40 minutes after 2 mg of IV lorazepam for agitation, continuous 20-25 Hz activity of about 30 µV is present, maximal frontocentrally, persisting into drowsiness with no clinical change. What is the most likely explanation?
questions.explanation: Benzodiazepines produce continuous, frontocentrally predominant beta (typically 15-25 Hz) that persists into drowsiness and light sleep. Generalized paroxysmal fast activity occurs in brief bursts, not continuously; muscle artifact is broader-band, spikier and lessens with drowsiness; spindles are waxing-waning 11-16 Hz bursts lasting seconds, not continuous 20-25 Hz activity.
questions.learningObjective: Recognise benzodiazepine-induced beta in an ICU recording.
options: Generalized paroxysmal fast activity of an emerging seizure
Frontalis and temporalis muscle artifact from agitation
Medication-induced beta activity from the benzodiazepine
Sleep spindles intruding as the patient becomes drowsy
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: After IV midazolam, a patient admitted after a fall shows diffuse 18-22 Hz beta of about 25 µV over the right hemisphere but only about 8 µV over the left. Impedances are 2-4 kΩ and symmetric, and there is no skull defect or craniotomy. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Drug-induced beta is generated by the cortex, so a consistent hemispheric reduction points to the side of LOWER amplitude: cortical dysfunction or an interposed collection such as a subdural hematoma (relevant after a fall). An irritative focus does not produce persistent hemispheric excess beta; an asymmetry of this size is not an expected drug effect; impedances are stated to be symmetric, and there is no breach to enhance the right side.
questions.learningObjective: Use asymmetry of drug-induced beta to lateralise dysfunction.
options: An irritative focus on the right generating excess fast activity
An expected drug-related asymmetry of no clinical significance
Reduced cortical beta on the left, as from a subdural collection
Higher right-sided impedance exaggerating the beta amplitude
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: You are starting cEEG on a 61-year-old on day 1 after an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. Targeted temperature management and a propofol infusion are running, and a neuromuscular blocker was given for shivering. Which set of history details is most important to record at hookup for interpretation?
questions.explanation: Temperature and sedative dose/timing directly change background continuity, amplitude and reactivity; a paralytic hides motor signs and muscle artifact; post-arrest patterns change with time since arrest. The other sets are relevant to cardiology, epilepsy history or overall prognosis but do not change how the current tracing must be read.
questions.learningObjective: Capture the history that confounds post-arrest EEG interpretation.

references.citation: ACNS Standardized Critical Care EEG Terminology: 2021 Version (Hirsch et al., J Clin Neurophysiol 2021)

options: Arrest rhythm, number of shocks given, and the admission blood pressure
Core temperature, sedative and paralytic doses with times, time since arrest
Prior seizure history, handedness, and any family history of epilepsy
Downtime estimate, bystander CPR, and the paramedics' arrival time
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A cEEG order reads: '61 y/o M s/p OHCA, on TTM 33 °C, GCS 5T, r/o NCSE.' Which reading of the order is correct?
questions.explanation: s/p = status post; OHCA = out-of-hospital cardiac arrest; TTM = targeted temperature management; the 'T' after a GCS score means intubated (verbal response not testable), not 'total'; NCSE = nonconvulsive status epilepticus. Misreading TTM as transcranial monitoring or NCSE as neurocardiogenic syncope changes the clinical question.
questions.learningObjective: Interpret common ICU order abbreviations.
options: Post out-of-hospital arrest; cooled; GCS total of 5; rule out nonconvulsive status epilepticus
Post out-of-hospital arrest; transcranial monitoring; intubated; rule out nonconvulsive status
Post out-of-hospital arrest; cooled; intubated; rule out nonconvulsive status epilepticus
Post out-of-hospital arrest; cooled; intubated; rule out neurocardiogenic syncope episodes
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: An order reads: 'SAH, H-H grade 4, POD 6 s/p aneurysm coiling, EVD in situ, on nimodipine. cEEG for DCI surveillance.' What is the cEEG primarily intended to detect?
questions.explanation: SAH = subarachnoid hemorrhage, H-H = Hunt-Hess, POD = postoperative day, EVD = external ventricular drain, DCI = delayed cerebral ischemia, which usually develops in the first two weeks after aneurysmal SAH. cEEG changes such as loss of faster frequencies or new focal slowing can precede clinical deterioration. The distractors misread SAH as subdural, DCI as a drug effect, or the drain as the target.
questions.learningObjective: Decode a neurocritical care cEEG indication.
options: Delayed cerebral ischemia from vasospasm after subarachnoid hemorrhage
Diffuse cortical irritation from blood products after subdural hemorrhage
Drug-induced encephalopathy from the nimodipine infusion after surgery
Drainage-catheter injury from the external ventricular drain placement
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: For refractory status epilepticus, a pentobarbital infusion is started at a low dose and increased stepwise. In a patient whose EEG began with a continuous background, which sequence of EEG changes is expected as the dose rises?
questions.explanation: Barbiturates and other anesthetics first increase beta at low doses, then produce diffuse slowing, then burst suppression with lengthening interburst intervals, and finally suppression at the highest doses. The other sequences put beta after slowing or burst suppression before slowing, which is the wrong dose order.
questions.learningObjective: Predict dose-dependent anesthetic EEG changes.
options: Diffuse slowing, then increased beta, then burst suppression, then suppression
Increased beta, then burst suppression, then diffuse slowing, then suppression
Burst suppression, then increased beta, then diffuse slowing, then suppression
Increased beta, then diffuse slowing, then burst suppression, then suppression
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: At cEEG hookup the nurse reports that a continuous cisatracurium infusion was started 20 minutes ago for ventilator dyssynchrony. Why is this important to record in the history?
questions.explanation: Neuromuscular blockers act at the neuromuscular junction: they do not alter cerebral activity, but they abolish clinical motor signs, so seizures can be purely electrographic, and they reduce muscle artifact, which changes how clean the record looks. They do not suppress the background, induce beta, or lower the seizure threshold.
questions.learningObjective: Know how paralytics affect the clinical and EEG picture.
options: It suppresses cortical activity, so a low-voltage background should be expected
It hides motor signs and muscle artifact but leaves cerebral activity unchanged
It produces diffuse beta activity that can mimic a benzodiazepine drug effect
It lowers the seizure threshold, so more frequent discharges should be expected
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: An EEG is requested to support a determination of brain death. The chart shows core temperature 36.4 °C, sodium 141 mmol/L, a pentobarbital infusion stopped 8 hours ago, and no paralytic since admission. Which history item most limits interpretation of an isoelectric record?
questions.explanation: Barbiturates have a long elimination half-life and can produce a reversible isoelectric EEG, so a recent infusion is a major confounder (drug levels need to be addressed). 36.4 °C is normothermic and a sodium of 141 mmol/L is normal; the absence of a paralytic is not a confounder of inactivity.
questions.learningObjective: Identify drug confounders before an ECI recording.

references.citation: ACNS Guideline 3: Minimum Technical Standards for EEG Recording in Suspected Cerebral Death (Stecker et al., J Clin Neurophysiol 2016)

options: The core temperature, which is too low for the record to be interpretable
The sodium value, which is in a range that suppresses cortical activity
The recent pentobarbital infusion, which can suppress cortical activity
The absence of a paralytic, so muscle artifact may obscure the record
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A patient with subarachnoid hemorrhage needs 5 days of cEEG and is expected to have repeated head CT scans and possibly an MRI. Which electrode plan best supports continuous recording through imaging?
questions.explanation: CT/MR-conditional conductive plastic electrodes and leads cause little CT streak artifact and can stay on under the manufacturer's conditions, preserving monitoring. Repeated removal creates gaps and skin trauma; nonferrous metal still causes CT streak artifact and can heat in MRI; needles are metal and add infection and skin risk over days.
questions.learningObjective: Choose electrodes for prolonged cEEG with imaging.
options: Gold cup electrodes with collodion, removed and reapplied for each scan
Silver-silver chloride cups, since any nonferrous metal is imaging-safe
Imaging-compatible conductive plastic electrodes with compatible leads
Subdermal needle electrodes, taped flat so they stay out of the field
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A ventilated ICU patient shows monomorphic 5-Hz activity of constant frequency and amplitude in nearly all channels for 40 minutes, without evolution. The ventilator is a high-frequency oscillator set to 5 Hz. What is the most likely explanation?
questions.explanation: Activity whose frequency exactly matches the oscillator setting, unchanged for 40 minutes and present in nearly every channel without a physiological field, is mechanical artifact. A seizure would show evolution; cerebral rhythmic activity would not lock to the ventilator setting; mains aliasing to exactly 5 Hz would need an implausible sampling rate.
questions.learningObjective: Recognise high-frequency oscillatory ventilator artifact.
options: Generalized rhythmic theta of cerebral origin from encephalopathy
Mechanical artifact transmitted from the oscillatory ventilator
A nonconvulsive seizure with an unusually fixed 5-Hz frequency
Mains interference aliased down to 5 Hz by a low sampling rate
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Shortly after continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) is started, low-amplitude sharp transients recur about every 0.8 s in many channels, largest where impedances are highest. The CRRT blood pump sits beside the head of the bed. What is the best next step?
questions.explanation: Onset with CRRT, a fixed rate, and prominence at high-impedance electrodes suggest artifact from the roller pump; confirming time-locking and then reducing pickup (lead routing, lower and balanced impedances) addresses the source. A filter change distorts the record without fixing the cause; labelling them as discharges risks misinterpretation; stopping dialysis is not the technologist's decision.
questions.learningObjective: Troubleshoot dialysis-pump artifact in cEEG.
options: Raise the low-frequency filter to 5 Hz so the transients are less prominent
Time them against the pump rotation, then reroute leads and lower impedances
Mark them as possible periodic discharges and continue standard review
Pause the CRRT circuit briefly so the recording can be checked without it
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Very narrow spikes (under 2 ms) appear in most channels at a fixed rate of 60/min. In the ECG channel, each spike precedes a wide QRS complex by a constant few milliseconds. What are they?
questions.explanation: A pacing stimulus is extremely brief, occurs at a fixed programmed rate and immediately precedes the paced (wide) QRS. Pulse artifact is a slow wave lagging the QRS by roughly 200 ms; ECG artifact coincides with the QRS and is broader; cerebral discharges last tens of milliseconds or more and are not time-locked to the ECG.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish pacemaker artifact from other cardiac artifacts.
options: Cardiac pacemaker stimulus artifact
Pulse artifact from a scalp artery
ECG artifact from each QRS complex
Generalized periodic discharges, 1 Hz
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A supine patient is on a bed with a lateral rotation therapy mode. Slow waves appear only in channels containing O1, O2, T5 and T6 and recur each time the bed tilts; frontal and central channels are clean. What is the most effective response?
questions.explanation: Waves confined to the electrodes the head rests on and time-locked to bed movement are movement artifact of dependent electrodes, best corrected at the source. A higher LFF distorts genuine slow activity without fixing the cause; re-referencing does not stop electrode motion; cerebral delta would not track the bed's tilt cycle.
questions.learningObjective: Localise and correct bed-related movement artifact.
options: Raise the low-frequency filter in all channels until the waves are reduced
Secure the posterior electrodes and leads, and stabilise the head on the pillow
Re-reference the montage to linked ears to cancel the posterior waves
Describe the waves as bilateral posterior rhythmic delta of cerebral origin
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Left temporal LPDs are reviewed in an ipsilateral ear-referenced montage. With each discharge, Fp1-A1, F3-A1, C3-A1, P3-A1 and O1-A1 all show a similar downward deflection of about 30 µV, while T3-A1 shows only a small upward one. Right-sided channels are flat. What best explains this?
questions.explanation: With negative-up convention, a downward deflection in X-A1 means A1 is more negative than X. Uniform, similar downward deflections in every channel sharing A1 mean the reference itself is active; T3, the discharge maximum, is only slightly more negative than the contaminated A1, so T3-A1 shows just a small upward deflection. A true parasagittal positivity would not be uniform; simultaneous lead reversal in five channels is implausible; a C3 maximum would deflect upward in C3-A1.
questions.learningObjective: Recognise an active ear reference from referential deflections.

references.citation: ACNS Guideline 6: A Proposal for Standard Montages to Be Used in Clinical EEG (Acharya et al., J Clin Neurophysiol 2016)

options: A positive field maximal over the left parasagittal electrodes
A1 is involved in the discharge, contaminating the left reference
Input leads reversed in all of the left parasagittal channels
A negative discharge maximal at C3, with relative sparing of T3
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Referential to a quiet noncephalic reference, a left-sided discharge measures Fp1 -10, F7 -30, T3 -90, T5 -50 and O1 -10 µV (negative values electronegative). With the standard convention (input 1 negative deflects up), what do F7-T3 and T3-T5 show in a longitudinal bipolar chain?
questions.explanation: Each channel shows input 1 minus input 2. F7-T3 = -30 - (-90) = +60 µV, so input 1 is relatively positive and the pen deflects down. T3-T5 = -90 - (-50) = -40 µV, so it deflects up: a phase reversal at T3. Reversing the signs ignores the convention; 120/140 µV adds instead of subtracting; two downward deflections miss the reversal.
questions.learningObjective: Derive bipolar deflections and phase reversal from referential values.
options: F7-T3: 60 µV up; T3-T5: 40 µV down
F7-T3: 120 µV down; T3-T5: 140 µV up
F7-T3: 60 µV down; T3-T5: 40 µV down
F7-T3: 60 µV down; T3-T5: 40 µV up
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: In a right parasagittal chain, recurring sharp transients show: Fp2-F4 flat, F4-C4 10 µV down, C4-P4 25 µV down and P4-O2 60 µV down, with no phase reversal. What is the best next step to localise the field?
questions.explanation: Deflections growing toward the last electrode without a reversal suggest an end-of-chain maximum (here near O2), which a bipolar chain cannot confirm. A referential montage with a quiet reference shows the amplitude at each electrode directly. Reversing the chain only inverts every deflection; sensitivity changes size, not reversals; a filter change alters waveform shape, not location.
questions.learningObjective: Resolve end-of-chain ambiguity with a referential montage.

references.citation: ACNS Guideline 6: A Proposal for Standard Montages to Be Used in Clinical EEG (Acharya et al., J Clin Neurophysiol 2016)

options: Reverse the chain to run O2-P4-C4-F4-Fp2 and look for a phase reversal
Repeat the same chain at higher sensitivity to reveal a hidden reversal
Raise the low-frequency filter to sharpen the transients for comparison
Review the same epoch in a referential montage with an uninvolved reference
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: For an electrocerebral inactivity recording in an adult with a nasion-inion distance of 34 cm, interelectrode distances of at least 10 cm are required. What are the approximate Cz-Pz and Fz-Pz distances along the midline, and which meets the requirement?
questions.explanation: Midline electrodes are 20% of the nasion-inion distance apart: Cz-Pz = 0.2 × 34 = 6.8 cm and Fz-Pz = 0.4 × 34 = 13.6 cm, so only the double-distance Fz-Pz derivation meets 10 cm. 3.4/6.8 cm uses 10% steps; 10.2 cm uses 30%; 13.6/27.2 cm doubles both.
questions.learningObjective: Apply the ECI interelectrode distance requirement.

references.citation: ACNS Guideline 3: Minimum Technical Standards for EEG Recording in Suspected Cerebral Death (Stecker et al., J Clin Neurophysiol 2016)

options: 6.8 cm and 13.6 cm; only Fz-Pz meets it
3.4 cm and 6.8 cm; neither pair meets it
10.2 cm and 13.6 cm; both pairs meet it
13.6 cm and 27.2 cm; both pairs meet it
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Twenty-two minutes into an electrocerebral inactivity recording, the settings are 7 µV/mm, LFF 1 Hz and HFF 15 Hz. Judged against ACNS minimum standards, which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: ACNS requires a sensitivity of 2 µV/mm for at least 30 minutes of recording, an HFF not below 30 Hz and an LFF not above 1 Hz. The 15-Hz HFF is too low, the 1-Hz LFF is acceptable, and time recorded at 7 µV/mm does not count toward the 30 minutes at 2 µV/mm.
questions.learningObjective: Check ECI settings and duration against ACNS standards.

references.citation: ACNS Guideline 3: Minimum Technical Standards for EEG Recording in Suspected Cerebral Death (Stecker et al., J Clin Neurophysiol 2016)

options: Change sensitivity only; then record 8 more minutes to reach 30
Change sensitivity, HFF and LFF; then record 8 more minutes
Change HFF and LFF only; then record 30 minutes at 7 µV/mm
Change sensitivity and HFF; then record 30 minutes at 2 µV/mm
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Before an electrocerebral inactivity recording, impedances are 1.5-6 kΩ and a calibration square wave is equal in all channels. Which additional check confirms that each electrode is connected and displayed in the expected channels?
questions.explanation: ACNS requires a test of system integrity: gently touching or tapping each electrode should produce artifact in exactly the channels that contain it, proving the electrode-to-display pathway. Calibration and biocalibration test the amplifiers, not individual electrode connections or montage mapping; repeated impedance checks do not show where each electrode is displayed.
questions.learningObjective: Perform the ECI integrity test.

references.citation: ACNS Guideline 3: Minimum Technical Standards for EEG Recording in Suspected Cerebral Death (Stecker et al., J Clin Neurophysiol 2016)

options: Repeat the calibration with a larger signal to confirm channel gain
Recheck all impedances after 10 minutes to confirm they are stable
Touch each electrode in turn and see an artifact in the right channels
Run a biological calibration with Fp1-O2 fed into every channel
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Preparing an electrocerebral inactivity study, impedances are 2-5 kΩ except F3 and C3, which both read about 60 Ω. The F3-C3 channel is nearly flat while neighbouring channels show low-level noise. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: ACNS specifies ECI impedances between 100 and 10,000 Ω: values below 100 Ω suggest a short between electrodes, which makes the shared channel artificially flat and could mimic inactivity. Open circuits give very high impedance and noise; a calibration fault would not change electrode impedance readings.
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a salt bridge from abnormally low impedance.

references.citation: ACNS Guideline 3: Minimum Technical Standards for EEG Recording in Suspected Cerebral Death (Stecker et al., J Clin Neurophysiol 2016)

options: Very good contact at F3 and C3 needing no change
Open circuits from broken F3 and C3 lead wires
A calibration fault in the F3 and C3 amplifiers
A paste or saline bridge that shorts F3 to C3
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: During an electrocerebral inactivity recording at 2 µV/mm, no cerebral activity is seen. So far the technologist has performed only a sternal rub. Which further testing meets ACNS minimum standards?
questions.explanation: The guideline calls for testing reactivity to intense somatosensory, auditory and visual stimuli, each marked on the recording. Photic flash rates and passive eye opening alone omit auditory and somatosensory testing; hyperventilation is not part of ECI testing; a benzodiazepine would add a confounder rather than test reactivity.
questions.learningObjective: Apply ECI stimulation requirements.

references.citation: ACNS Guideline 3: Minimum Technical Standards for EEG Recording in Suspected Cerebral Death (Stecker et al., J Clin Neurophysiol 2016)

options: Passive eye opening and closing, plus photic stimulation at 1-30 Hz
Hyperventilation via the ventilator, plus repeated sternal rubs
Intense auditory and visual stimuli, plus further noxious stimulation
A benzodiazepine challenge, plus repeated noxious stimulation
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: During an electrocerebral inactivity recording at 2 µV/mm, rhythmic waves of about 3 µV at 1.2 Hz are seen in many channels. The ECG channel shows a heart rate of 72/min and the ventilator rate is 14/min. What do these waves most likely represent?
questions.explanation: 72 beats per minute ÷ 60 = 1.2 Hz, matching the waves; time-locking to the ECG channel confirms pulse or ECG artifact. 14 breaths/min is about 0.23 Hz; artifact does not count as cerebral activity; aliasing of mains frequency to 1.2 Hz is implausible.
questions.learningObjective: Identify cardiac artifact at high sensitivity.

references.citation: ACNS Guideline 3: Minimum Technical Standards for EEG Recording in Suspected Cerebral Death (Stecker et al., J Clin Neurophysiol 2016)

options: Cardiac-related artifact matching the 72/min heart rate
Ventilator artifact matching the set 14/min breath rate
Residual cerebral delta activity that excludes inactivity
Mains interference aliased down to 1.2 Hz on the display
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: On day 3 of cEEG, abrupt steep deflections with slow decay appear intermittently in only F8-T4 and T4-T6. T4 impedance has risen to 28 kΩ while the others are under 5 kΩ. What is the best response?
questions.explanation: Deflections confined to the two channels sharing T4, with high T4 impedance, are electrode pops from a drying or loosening electrode. Re-preparing the site fixes the cause. Filtering or lowering sensitivity only masks the artifact and can hide real activity; omitting T4 sacrifices right temporal coverage in an ICU patient.
questions.learningObjective: Maintain electrode quality during prolonged cEEG.
options: Raise the low-frequency filter in the two affected channels to 5 Hz
Switch to a montage that leaves T4 out for the rest of the study
Re-prepare the T4 site, reapply the electrode and recheck impedance
Reduce the sensitivity of the two affected channels to 15 µV/mm
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: For overnight ICU video-EEG, the patient is intubated, the room lights are dimmed at 22:00, and a blanket covers the body to the chin. Which camera setup best supports later review of events?
questions.explanation: Review needs the face and limbs visible (subtle twitching, eye deviation) and usable images in the dark, which infrared provides without disturbing sleep. A face-only close-up misses limb movements; a covered body hides motor signs and full lighting disrupts care; dim ambient light gives unusable video.
questions.learningObjective: Set up ICU video for event characterisation.
options: Face in close-up for eye movements, infrared mode switched on at night
Whole bed in wide view with blanket in place, room lights left on fully
Face and limbs in view with blanket folded back, ambient light at night
Face and limbs in view with blanket folded back, infrared mode at night
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: During cEEG, a technologist at the bedside sees left-sided LPDs accelerate and evolve into rhythmic 3-Hz sharp activity over the left hemisphere. The patient's right hand begins twitching. What should the technologist do first?
questions.explanation: An evolving pattern with a contralateral motor correlate is a seizure: testing responsiveness during the event adds critical clinical information, and the team is alerted promptly. Restraining the limb obscures the clinical sign; impedance checks waste time on a cerebral event; waiting 5 minutes delays treatment.
questions.learningObjective: Respond to an evolving seizure during cEEG.

references.citation: ACNS Standardized Critical Care EEG Terminology: 2021 Version (Hirsch et al., J Clin Neurophysiol 2021)

options: Hold the twitching hand still, mark the event, and notify the team per protocol
Mark the event, check the right-hand impedances, then notify the team per protocol
Mark the event, and notify the team per protocol once it has lasted 5 minutes
Test responsiveness, mark the event, and notify the team per protocol
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A patient needs cEEG one day after a left frontotemporal craniotomy. The stapled incision runs across the F7 and T3 positions; the right side is intact. Which placement approach is best?
questions.explanation: Electrodes must avoid fresh incisions (infection and wound risk), coverage of the operated region should be kept, and moving homologous right-sided electrodes equally preserves valid left-right comparison. Placing over staples is unsafe; omission loses the region of most interest; asymmetric placement creates false amplitude asymmetries.
questions.learningObjective: Modify electrode placement around a surgical site.
options: Place F7 and T3 over the staples with extra paste, and document the placement
Shift F7 and T3 off the incision, mirror the shifts on the right, and document it
Omit F7 and T3, keep the right side standard, and document the omitted sites
Shift F7 and T3 off the incision, keep the right standard, and document it
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A cEEG spectrogram shows brief increases in power from 2 to 20 Hz every 15-20 minutes overnight. The nursing notes record repositioning every 2 hours. What should the technologist do when reviewing these trend changes?
questions.explanation: Quantitative trends flag candidate events but cannot by themselves distinguish seizures from artifact or arousals; each change must be checked in the raw EEG and video. The 15-20 minute recurrence does not match 2-hourly turns, so assuming artifact is unsafe; rescaling hides rather than explains the changes.
questions.learningObjective: Verify quantitative EEG trend changes against raw EEG.
options: Count each change as a seizure, since the spectrogram is a seizure screen
Count each change as turning artifact, since nursing care is recorded
Check the raw EEG and video at each change to decide what it represents
Adjust the spectrogram colour scale until the changes no longer stand out
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: In an average-reference montage of 19 electrodes, a 500-µV electrode artifact occurs at T4. Every other channel shows a simultaneous inverted deflection of about 26 µV. What is the best fix?
questions.explanation: The average includes T4: 500 ÷ 19 ≈ 26 µV, which appears inverted in every other channel. Excluding the bad electrode from the average (or using a bipolar montage) stops the contamination. The deflections are not a cerebral field; lowering sensitivity shrinks all activity equally; adding two electrodes only reduces the contamination to about 24 µV.
questions.learningObjective: Recognise and correct average-reference contamination.

references.citation: ACNS Guideline 6: A Proposal for Standard Montages to Be Used in Clinical EEG (Acharya et al., J Clin Neurophysiol 2016)

options: Read the 26-µV deflections as a widespread field of opposite polarity
Reduce sensitivity in all channels so the 26-µV deflections shrink
Exclude T4 from the average, or review it in a bipolar montage
Add the ear electrodes to the average so the 26-µV effect is diluted
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A febrile ICU patient (39.2 °C) develops very slow 0.3-Hz undulations of up to 150 µV in frontal and temporal channels over 30 minutes, while impedances drift downward. What is the most likely cause and best response?
questions.explanation: Fever, very slow (about 0.25-0.5 Hz) high-amplitude undulations and falling impedances indicate sweat artifact, corrected by cooling and drying the skin and re-preparing sites. Cerebral delta does not lower impedance; glossokinetic artifact needs tongue movement; a ventilator at 18/min would also give 0.3 Hz but would not explain falling impedances in febrile skin.
questions.learningObjective: Recognise and correct sweat artifact in the ICU.
options: Frontal rhythmic delta; mark it as a new encephalopathic pattern
Sweat artifact; cool and dry the skin and re-prepare the affected sites
Glossokinetic artifact; ask the nurse to suction oral secretions
Ventilator artifact; ask the therapist to change the breathing rate
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Generalized 4-Hz rhythmic, sharply contoured activity appears abruptly in all channels, lasts 3 minutes and stops abruptly, with no change in frequency. Video shows a therapist beside the bed with hands on the patient's chest at that time. What is the most likely explanation?
questions.explanation: Abrupt onset and offset, unchanging frequency, involvement of all channels and a video showing chest percussion indicate mechanical artifact. A seizure would evolve; stimulus-induced arousal would not start and stop abruptly with a fixed frequency; shivering produces fast muscle activity rather than monomorphic 4-Hz waves.
questions.learningObjective: Use video to identify physiotherapy artifact.
options: Chest percussion artifact from respiratory physiotherapy
A generalized electrographic seizure without clinical signs
Generalized rhythmic theta from arousal to the stimulation
Shivering muscle artifact provoked by uncovering the chest
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A cEEG review screen shows 20 s per page across 300 mm. Lateralized periodic discharges recur every 18 mm. What is their frequency?
questions.explanation: 300 mm per 20 s = 15 mm/s, so 18 mm = 1.2 s between discharges, i.e. about 0.83 Hz. 1.7 Hz assumes 30 mm/s (0.6 s period); 1.2 Hz reports the period as a frequency; 0.6 Hz reports the 30-mm/s period as a frequency.
questions.learningObjective: Measure periodic discharge frequency at the actual display speed.
options: About 0.8 Hz
About 1.7 Hz
About 1.2 Hz
About 0.6 Hz
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A comatose patient has GPDs averaging 0.7 Hz with superimposed rhythmic fast activity (+F), present for hours without evolution and without a clinical correlate. How should this be classified under ACNS 2021?
questions.explanation: ACNS 2021 places PDs averaging 0.5-1 Hz in the ictal-interictal continuum when they have a plus modifier or fluctuation. Frequency below 1 Hz alone does not exclude IIC; duration cannot make a non-ictal pattern ESE; +F is a modifier, not a seizure criterion (seizures need >2.5 Hz discharges or definite evolution for at least 10 s).
questions.learningObjective: Apply ACNS IIC criteria to slow PDs with plus features.

references.citation: ACNS Standardized Critical Care EEG Terminology: 2021 Version (Hirsch et al., J Clin Neurophysiol 2021)

options: IIC, because 0.5-1-Hz PDs carry a plus modifier
Not IIC, because the PD frequency is below 1 Hz
ESE, because the pattern has persisted for hours
ESz, because rhythmic fast activity is superimposed
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Over a 60-minute cEEG epoch, a patient has five electrographic seizures lasting 2, 3, 3, 2 and 4 minutes, with no clinical signs. Under ACNS 2021, how should this hour be classified?
questions.explanation: Electrographic status epilepticus is at least 10 continuous minutes OR seizures totalling at least 20% of any 60-minute period. 14/60 ≈ 23%, so this hour qualifies. The 10-minute rule is only one route; 30% is not the threshold; the 5-minute rule applies to convulsive status, not ESE.
questions.learningObjective: Calculate seizure burden against the ESE definition.

references.citation: ACNS Standardized Critical Care EEG Terminology: 2021 Version (Hirsch et al., J Clin Neurophysiol 2021)

options: Not ESE, since no single seizure lasts 10 minutes or more
Not ESE, since the 14 minutes is under 30% of that hour
ESE only if any one seizure has lasted 5 minutes or more
ESE, since seizures total 14 minutes, over 20% of the hour
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A critically ill patient has runs of focal right frontal rhythmic activity starting at 5 Hz and speeding to 7 Hz, each lasting 6-8 s, with no clinical signs. Which ACNS 2021 term fits best?
questions.explanation: BIRDs are runs of rhythmic activity faster than 4 Hz (at least 6 waves) lasting 0.5 to under 10 s; they are 'definite' if they show evolution or resemble the patient's seizures, and 'possible' if they are sharply contoured without evolution. Evolution does not make them seizures unless it lasts at least 10 s; LRDA is delta-range (up to 4 Hz) activity, not 5-7 Hz.
questions.learningObjective: Classify brief evolving rhythmic runs.

references.citation: ACNS Standardized Critical Care EEG Terminology: 2021 Version (Hirsch et al., J Clin Neurophysiol 2021)

options: Possible BIRDs, as the runs last under 10 s
Definite BIRDs, as the runs show evolution
Electrographic seizures, as the runs evolve
LRDA with a plus modifier, as it is rhythmic
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Two days after cardiac arrest, off sedation, bursts alternate with interburst segments that deflect about 1 mm at 7 µV/mm. Interburst segments make up about 70% of the record. Which ACNS 2021 background term fits?
questions.explanation: 1 mm × 7 µV/mm = 7 µV, below 10 µV, so the interburst segments are suppression rather than attenuation. Suppression/attenuation occupying 50-99% of the record is burst suppression (or burst attenuation if ≥10 µV); 10-49% is discontinuous; a suppressed background has essentially no bursts.
questions.learningObjective: Grade background continuity using ACNS amplitude and percentage criteria.

references.citation: ACNS Standardized Critical Care EEG Terminology: 2021 Version (Hirsch et al., J Clin Neurophysiol 2021)

options: Burst attenuation
Burst suppression
Discontinuous background
Suppressed background
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Two days after a traumatic brain injury, a comatose patient off sedation shows 12-14 Hz spindles, vertex waves and K-complexes on a slow background, with clear changes on stimulation. Which pattern is this?
questions.explanation: Sleep-like elements (spindles, vertex waves, K-complexes) in a comatose patient form the spindle coma pattern, which is often reactive. Alpha coma is monotonous, usually unreactive 8-13 Hz activity; normal N2 sleep requires an arousable patient; a drug-related beta pattern is unlikely off sedation and lacks K-complexes.
questions.learningObjective: Recognise spindle coma.
options: Spindle coma pattern
Alpha coma pattern
Normal stage N2 sleep
Drug-related beta coma
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Four ICU patients are recorded off sedation. Which EEG indicates the most severe diffuse encephalopathy?
questions.explanation: Severity increases as the posterior rhythm is lost, slowing becomes continuous and lower in frequency, voltage falls and reactivity disappears. A slowed but reactive posterior rhythm with intermittent theta is mild; reactive theta-delta without a PDR is moderate; an 8-Hz PDR with intermittent frontal rhythmic delta is mild.
questions.learningObjective: Rank diffuse slowing by severity.
options: Reactive 7-Hz posterior rhythm with intermittent diffuse theta
Reactive mixed theta and delta with no posterior dominant rhythm
8-Hz posterior rhythm with intermittent frontal rhythmic delta
Low-voltage, unreactive, continuous 1-2 Hz polymorphic delta
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Periodic discharges occur independently and asynchronously at T3, at T4 and at O2, each at about 1 Hz. Under ACNS 2021 Main term 1, how are they described?
questions.explanation: Multifocal requires at least three independent locations with at least one in each hemisphere: T3 (left), T4 and O2 (right). BIPDs describe two independent foci, one per hemisphere; GPDs are bisynchronous and symmetric; LPDs are unilateral or bilateral synchronous but asymmetric.
questions.learningObjective: Apply ACNS Main term 1 to independent PDs.

references.citation: ACNS Standardized Critical Care EEG Terminology: 2021 Version (Hirsch et al., J Clin Neurophysiol 2021)

options: Multifocal PDs (MfPDs)
Bilateral independent PDs (BIPDs)
Generalized PDs (GPDs)
Lateralized PDs (LPDs)
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Periodic discharges at 1 Hz appear simultaneously over both hemispheres but are consistently about three times higher in amplitude over the left. Under ACNS 2021 Main term 1, how should they be classified?
questions.explanation: ACNS 'lateralized' includes unilateral patterns and bilateral synchronous patterns that are clearly and consistently asymmetric; 'generalized' requires bilateral, bisynchronous and symmetric discharges. BIPDs are two independent (asynchronous) lateralized patterns, not synchronous ones.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish lateralized from generalized PDs.

references.citation: ACNS Standardized Critical Care EEG Terminology: 2021 Version (Hirsch et al., J Clin Neurophysiol 2021)

options: LPDs, as synchronous but asymmetric PDs count as lateralized
GPDs, as any bilateral synchronous PDs count as generalized
BIPDs, as both hemispheres are involved at the same time
GPDs, since bilateral asymmetry is only noted as a comment
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A patient with altered awareness has continuous 2-Hz GPDs for 40 minutes. After IV lorazepam the GPDs resolve within minutes and the patient begins following commands. Under ACNS 2021, how is the pre-treatment pattern best classified?
questions.explanation: 2-Hz GPDs alone fall in the ictal-interictal continuum, but ACNS 2021 counts a pattern as an electroclinical seizure when both the EEG and the clinical state improve with a parenteral antiseizure medication; lasting over 10 minutes, it is electroclinical status. 'Possible' ECSE applies when only the EEG improves; ESE requires >2.5 Hz discharges or evolution.
questions.learningObjective: Interpret an antiseizure medication trial with ACNS terms.

references.citation: ACNS Standardized Critical Care EEG Terminology: 2021 Version (Hirsch et al., J Clin Neurophysiol 2021)

options: Possible electroclinical status epilepticus
Electroclinical status epilepticus
Ictal-interictal continuum only
Electrographic status epilepticus
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A confused patient with hepatic failure has GPDs of triphasic morphology averaging 1.5 Hz for most of a 2-hour recording, with an anterior-posterior lag and no evolution. How should the pattern be classified under ACNS 2021?
questions.explanation: ACNS 2021 describes these as GPDs with triphasic morphology; PDs averaging more than 1 Hz and up to 2.5 Hz for at least 10 s fall in the ictal-interictal continuum regardless of morphology or suspected metabolic cause. 'Triphasic waves' is no longer a separate term; without >2.5 Hz or evolution they are not ESE; being below 2.5 Hz does not make 1.5-Hz PDs simply interictal.
questions.learningObjective: Apply IIC criteria to GPDs with triphasic morphology.

references.citation: ACNS Standardized Critical Care EEG Terminology: 2021 Version (Hirsch et al., J Clin Neurophysiol 2021)

options: Metabolic triphasic waves, a category outside ACNS terms
ESE, as the GPDs are continuous for more than 10 minutes
Interictal GPDs, since the frequency is below 2.5 Hz
IIC; triphasic morphology does not exclude this category
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: On day 4 of cEEG, you find a 5-mm blistered, reddened area under the O2 electrode of a patient on vasopressors. Other sites look intact. What is the best action?
questions.explanation: Injured skin must be offloaded: the electrode is moved, all other sites are inspected because the same risk applies, and the finding is recorded and passed to nursing promptly for wound care. Reapplying at the same site or leaving it worsens the injury; deferring documentation and communication delays care.
questions.learningObjective: Manage electrode-related skin injury during cEEG.
options: Reapply O2 at the same spot with fresh paste and gauze, then document the finding
Leave O2 in place until the study ends, then document and report the skin finding
Move O2 to an intact nearby site and document the finding at the end of the study
Move O2 to an intact nearby site, inspect all sites, document and inform the nurse
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A patient on cEEG with gold cup electrodes is called for an urgent MRI. The electrodes and leads are not labelled MR-conditional. What is the correct approach?
questions.explanation: Conductive metal electrodes and leads can heat and burn the skin through radiofrequency induction even when non-ferromagnetic, and they degrade images. Equipment not labelled MR-conditional must not enter the scanner; disconnecting or taping leads does not prevent heating.
questions.learningObjective: Apply MRI safety to EEG electrodes.
options: Disconnect the head box only and leave the cups on, per MRI safety protocol
Tape the leads away from the head and the coil, per MRI safety protocol
Take off the electrodes and leads before transport, per MRI safety protocol
Leave the cups on, since gold is nonmagnetic, per MRI safety protocol
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: You complete a cEEG hookup on a patient under contact (enteric) precautions for Clostridioides difficile. After taking off gown and gloves, how should you clean your hands?
questions.explanation: C. difficile spores resist alcohol, so soap-and-water handwashing (mechanical removal) is required after contact. Alcohol rub is preferred for most organisms but not spores; gloves do not replace hand hygiene; chlorhexidine skin wipes are not sporicidal hand hygiene.
questions.learningObjective: Apply hand hygiene for spore-forming organisms.
options: Use alcohol rub, as it is the preferred method for all organisms
Use alcohol rub, then put on fresh gloves before leaving the room
Use a chlorhexidine skin wipe, as it is sporicidal for C. difficile
Wash with soap and water, as alcohol rub does not kill the spores
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: You need to lift and turn the head of an ICU patient to place posterior electrodes. The patient has an open external ventricular drain levelled at the tragus and a right internal jugular central line. What should you do first?
questions.explanation: Moving the head changes the drain's reference level and can cause over- or under-drainage of CSF; clamping and levelling are nursing/physician tasks, so the technologist coordinates before moving the patient. Adjusting the drain is outside scope; turning with the drain open is the hazard; omitting posterior electrodes loses needed coverage.
questions.learningObjective: Coordinate head positioning around an external ventricular drain.
options: Re-level the drain to the new head position yourself before turning
Turn the head away from the central line, keeping the drain open
Ask the nurse to clamp or manage the drain before the head is moved
Place only anterior electrodes so that the head need not be moved
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: At 03:12 you phone the on-call neurologist about new electrographic seizures on cEEG. Which log entry is most complete?
questions.explanation: Critical-result communication records when it happened, who received it, what was communicated and confirmation that it was understood (read-back). Each distractor omits either the recipient, the time or the confirmation.
questions.learningObjective: Document critical-result communication completely.
options: Time, the neurologist's name, what was reported, and their read-back
Time, the seizure count, and that the finding was reported by phone
The neurologist's name, what was reported, and the next review time
Time, what was reported, and that the bedside nurse was also told
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: At 02:40 you page the on-call neurologist about a pattern meeting criteria for electrographic status epilepticus. After 15 minutes a second page is also unanswered. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation: Electrographic status epilepticus is time-critical; when the primary contact is unreachable, the chain of command is followed so a physician acts promptly. Continued paging of the same person, waiting for morning or sending an email delays treatment.
questions.learningObjective: Escalate unacknowledged critical findings.

references.citation: ACNS Standardized Critical Care EEG Terminology: 2021 Version (Hirsch et al., J Clin Neurophysiol 2021)

options: Keep paging the same neurologist every 15 minutes per policy
Escalate to the next physician in the chain of command per policy
Note it in the log and leave it for the morning reader per policy
Email the finding to the neurologist and morning team per policy
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: The bedside monitor clock runs 4 minutes ahead of the EEG system clock. The nurse charts IV lorazepam at 14:05 by the bedside clock. Where should the annotation be placed in the EEG?
questions.explanation: If the bedside clock is 4 minutes ahead, 14:05 bedside corresponds to 14:01 on the EEG clock. Using 14:05 or adding the offset (14:09) misplaces the event; anchoring to the first EEG change assumes the drug's effect rather than recording when it was given.
questions.learningObjective: Correct event annotations for clock offsets.
options: At 14:01 EEG time, noting the clock offset
At 14:05 EEG time, as charted by the nurse
At 14:09 EEG time, noting the clock offset
At the first EEG change after 14:05 EEG time
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Four patients are on day 3 of cEEG with collodion-applied electrodes. Whose scalp is at greatest risk of electrode-related pressure injury?
questions.explanation: Pressure injury risk rises with immobility (sedation, supine head on electrodes), poor tissue perfusion (vasopressors) and edema. Each distractor has only one or two of these factors, and regular turning or being awake and upright reduces sustained pressure.
questions.learningObjective: Identify patients at highest risk of electrode skin injury.
options: Supine, sedated, normotensive, turned every 2 hours
Supine, sedated, on vasopressors, with scalp edema
Drowsy, turned 2-hourly, febrile, with mild scalp edema
Awake, sitting up, on vasopressors, with an intact scalp
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)

questions.stem: During cEEG in an ICU, all channels suddenly become suppressed, and the ECG channel shows a disorganized irregular waveform without QRS complexes. No staff are at the bedside. What should you do first?
questions.explanation: Sudden diffuse suppression with a disorganized ECG lacking QRS complexes suggests ventricular fibrillation and cerebral hypoperfusion: a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate help. Equipment checks, annotation or rechecking leads first delay resuscitation; the EEG change itself supports a real event.
questions.learningObjective: Recognise and act on a cardiac arrest seen on cEEG.
options: Call for help and activate the emergency response at the bedside
Check the head box and amplifier connections for a technical fault
Annotate the change and begin reviewing the preceding hour of EEG
Recheck ECG lead placement before raising any alarm about it
questions.author: NeuroLinea challenge batch 8 (AI-drafted; requires expert review)
